items.title: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
items.summary: Thursday's meeting between the leaders of US, China and Russia will give Vladimir Putin a big stage - but it does not bring him closer to winning the war in Ukraine.
items.content:
Image caption, Nearly five years after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine turned him into a pariah, Putin is back on the global stage
But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin.
Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.
Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down â just the three of them â for talks.
That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.
It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed.
"We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.
But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.
It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.
One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.
In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."
Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.
Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.
Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States â Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe.
"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.
It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".
In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.
Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.
Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula â carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.
The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.
It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.
The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.
It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

items.summary: Gold Falls Below $3,800 as Federal Reserve Rate Hike Expectations Pressure Precious Metals  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
Gold Falls Below $3,800 as Federal Reserve Rate Hike Expectations Pressure Precious Metals
Small gold nugget ©Hans Gold prices extended their losses on Wednesday, falling below $3,800 per ounce and approaching their lowest levels in 14 months as expectations of further interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve weighed on precious metals.
At 00:48 ET (05:48 GMT), spot gold declined 1.5% to $3,790.18 per ounce, while US gold futures fell 1.1% to $3,823.67.
The decline followed comments from Federal Reserve officials indicating that additional monetary tightening may be necessary to bring inflation back towards the central bank's 2% target.
A stronger US dollar and elevated Treasury yields added to pressure on bullion, which does not generate interest income.
Gold Reaches Lowest Closing Level Since September 2025
Gold had ended the previous session 0.2% lower, recording its weakest closing level since September 2025.
The precious metal has lost more than 25% of its value since the conflict between the United States and Iran began in late February, as rising energy costs and inflation prompted expectations of tighter monetary policy.
The US dollar index rose 0.1% to 103.65, increasing the cost of dollar-denominated gold for investors holding other currencies.
Meanwhile, benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields remained above 5%, approaching their longest sustained period at that level in almost two decades.
Higher bond yields can reduce demand for non-yielding assets such as gold, particularly when investors expect interest rates to remain elevated.
Federal Reserve Officials Signal Further Monetary Tightening
Recent statements from Federal Reserve policymakers reinforced expectations that additional interest rate increases could be required.
St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem indicated that the US economy would probably need several further rate increases before spring.
New York Federal Reserve President John Williams also suggested that policymakers had more work to do to return inflation to the central bank's 2% objective.
Financial markets were pricing in 25-basis-point rate increases in December and January, followed by another adjustment by April.
Investors were awaiting the minutes of the Federal Reserve's October policy meeting, scheduled for publication later on Wednesday, for additional information about the outlook for borrowing costs.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh had avoided discussing interest rates directly in remarks earlier in the week, instead addressing possible economic developments associated with artificial intelligence.
Other precious metals followed gold lower during Wednesday's trading.
Silver fell 0.8% to $47.0145 per ounce, while platinum declined 0.5% to $1,424.45.
Spot palladium dropped 0.7% to $965.10 per ounce, and palladium futures decreased 0.9% to $963.00.
The declines reflected broader pressure across precious metals as investors assessed the implications of higher interest rates and a stronger dollar.
Analysts at ANZ said bargain buying following the recent decline could provide some support for gold prices.
However, the bank warned that further monetary tightening and a possible recovery in equity markets could reduce investment flows into bullion.
ANZ's central forecast assumes three 25-basis-point interest rate increases in December, January and March.
The bank nevertheless cautioned that it "cannot rule out a 50bp hike next month."
With financial markets pricing in approximately 80 basis points of additional tightening over the current cycle, ANZ said further rate increases could extend gold's near-term correction.
Despite the recent decline, ANZ maintained a positive medium- to long-term outlook for gold.
The bank expects political uncertainty surrounding US government funding, debt negotiations and fiscal policy to support demand for bullion as a portfolio diversification asset.
ANZ anticipates that renewed purchases by institutional and retail investors could establish support for gold prices around $3,600 per ounce.
The bank also maintained its projection that gold could reach $4,800 per ounce in 2027.
These expectations suggest that ANZ considers the current weakness temporary, although further Federal Reserve tightening remains a potential risk to prices in the coming months.
Gold Market Focuses on Fed Minutes and Interest Rate Outlook
Wednesday's decline highlighted the influence of monetary policy expectations on precious metals.
Gold's fall to $3,790.18 per ounce coincided with a stronger US dollar, elevated Treasury yields and expectations of additional Federal Reserve rate increases.
Investors will continue monitoring inflation data, central bank communications and developments in financial markets for indications of when demand for gold might stabilise.

items.content:
Emergency alerts and $75,000 rewards: South Korea fights exam cheating
South Korea plans to send emergency alerts before the first session of Thursday’s college entrance exam to detect concealed phones.
South Korean President has proposed financial rewards to encourage people to report exam cheating.
Banks, government offices and private businesses have been asked to delay their opening hours to ease traffic congestion for test takers.
SEOUL, SOUTH KOREA - NOVEMBER 18: South Korean students take their College Scholastic Ability Test at a school on November 18, 2021 in Seoul, South Korea. The annual College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), slated for Novemer 18 this year, is the country's most important annual academic event, and the whole country almost grinds to a halt for the smooth administration of the test. A total of 509,821 have applied for the CSAT this year, according to education authorities. About 490,000 high school seniors and graduates sit for the examinations at 1,300 test centers across the country, where academic records are all important. Success in the exam, one of the most rigourous standardized tests in the world, enables students to study at Korea's top universities. (Photo by Chung Sung-Jun/Getty Images)
South Korea plans to send emergency alerts to expose concealed phones, while offering rewards of at least $75,000 for reporting cheaters, as it gears for a key college entrance exam.
The measures, announced by President Lee Jae Myung in a post on X, come ahead of the country's annual college entrance exam, known as the Suneung, on Thursday which is expected to draw about 550,000 students, according to local media reports.
Emergency alerts are to be sent to mobile phones of all South Korean residents before the exam begins, aimed at identifying mobile phones that students fail to surrender, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said Tuesday.
"Even the most brazen examinee wouldn't be foolish enough to get caught when a hidden communication device rings during the exam, would they?" Lee said in an X post on Tuesday, adding that he had instructed officials to consider sending the emergency alerts periodically during the exam.
The tougher measures come after cheating cases involving smart glasses and miniature cameras in other national examinations raised concerns about the use of advanced technology in South Korea's college entrance exam.
The government is tightening inspections of electronic devices, including smart glasses, miniature cameras and wireless earbuds, Han said.
All students will be required to have their glasses inspected, while stickers will be placed over clothing buttons to prevent hidden cameras from being used. Authorities have deployed about 75,000 exam supervisors across 1,312 testing centers, with an additional 8,400 personnel assigned to inspect smart devices, monitor hallways and detect suspicious communication signals, according to Han.
South Korea's National Police Agency will be on heightened alert from 6 a.m. Thursday until further notice, Yonhap News reported, citing the agency. All officers will be required to maintain emergency communication channels to respond swiftly to any incidents, according to the report.
Lee also said AI companies had agreed to provide records of users who photograph exam questions and use AI for answers. He instructed officials to pursue legislation requiring companies to hand over records of suspected illegal requests for exam answers when requested by the government.
The government is also seeking to increase the period during which students caught cheating can be barred from retaking the exam from one year to 10 years, while serious cases could lead to criminal prosecution, Han said.
The exam will disrupt business activity across South Korea, with stock markets, banks and airlines adjusting their schedules.
Banks across South Korea will also open an hour later, operating from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., according to the Korea Federation of Banks. Some branches with flexible operating hours may follow different schedules.
The country's stock markets will open an hour later than usual at 10 a.m. Thursday and close at 4:30 p.m. while 130 flights will have their schedules adjusted as authorities temporarily restrict aircraft takeoffs and landings for 35 minutes during the English listening test.
Government offices and businesses have also been asked to delay their start times until 10 a.m. or later to ease traffic congestion for test takers, according to the Ministry of Education.

Pentagon Official Says Ukraine War Likely To Last Through Winter, Despite Mediation Efforts
Pentagon Official Says Ukraine War Likely To Last Through Winter, Despite Mediation Efforts
Utility workers repair a bridge in Kyiv closed to all traffic on November 17 following Russian missile attacks on the Ukrainian capital.
BRUSSELS -- A top Pentagon official told NATO allies that Moscow is likely to continue its war efforts in Ukraine at least through the winter months, despite Washington's attempts to secure a cease-fire and peace deal between Russia and Ukraine.
US Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby, speaking to alliance members in Brussels on November 17, also faced sharp pushback from US and Ukrainian allies for remarks critical of Kyiv's recent strikes deep inside Russia.
Colby was speaking at a gathering of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, an informal alliance of some 50 nations that coordinates military support for Ukraine among Western allies. It is also referred to as the Ramstein group for the US air base in Germany were talks were first held.
The defense undersecretary said that "as winter sets in, it appears that Russia will continue to generate more manpower and mobilize its war economy for the long haul," adding that all must be prepared for the conflict "to endure."
Crimea Bridge Critically Damaged As Ukraine, Russia Exchange Strikes
Colby said US President Donald Trump remains "firmly committed to bringing this conflict to an end on terms that secure a durable peace."
Trump is expected to attend a meeting in the Chinese city of Shenzhen together with Russian President Vladimir Putin and the Chinese leader Xi Jinping in which the war and various attempts to end it is expected to be discussed.
Trump's peace envoys, son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, are on the same day expected to attend a meeting in Berlin with the Coalition of the Willing -- a grouping led by Germany, France, and Britain set up to support Washington's mediation efforts and potentially form a peacekeeping mission should a cease-fire be agreed upon in Ukraine.
Colby also criticized Ukraine’s recent so-called deep strikes in Russian territories that has targeted both Russian energy facilities and the warehouses of the Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries.
"Our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war nor do they contribute to blunting Russia's advances on the front line," Colby said.
US Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby received pushback from US allies after criticizing Ukraine for attacks deep inside Russia. (file photo)
"Moreover, such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure, such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate."
He added, however, that "Ukraine should not be forced to fight with its hands tied behind its back," underlining that strikes "focused on the front line and direct support to that battle area is, of course," a different matter.
Ukraine Says Starshield Restrictions Persist, Hampering Drone Defenses
His comments come as Ukraine struck the strategic and symbolic Kerch Bridge, connecting mainland Russia with the illegally annexed Ukrainian Crimean Peninsula, severely disrupting Kremlin efforts to supply the occupied region. The bridge is the only direct road and rail link between Russia and the Black Sea peninsula.
Kyiv has struck at targets inside Russia in response to intensified Kremlin attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, including energy facilities, creating fuel shortages ahead of the likely brutal winter months.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskiy told RFE/RL on November 16 that Russia's efforts are aimed at "breaking the spirit" of its people as winter approaches.
Colby's remarks blasting Ukraine's strikes deep inside Russia were rejected by US and Ukrainian allies.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius rejected the criticism as "quite a stupid thing."
"Instead of criticizing Ukraine's deep strikes, better to criticize terrorist strikes every night and every day on energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine," he told reporters, citing relentless Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian sites.
British defense chief Wes Streeting echoed those remarks, saying Ukraine's strikes "helped to degrade Putin's war machine, buying time and saving lives."

He previously worked as RFE/RL's Brussels correspondent, covering numerous international summits, European elections, and international court rulings. He has reported from most European capitals, as well as Central Asia.

items.title: Senators press acting U.S. Navy Secretary on Iran war costs, sailor health in confirmation hearing - CNBC
items.summary: Senators press acting U.S. Navy Secretary on Iran war costs, sailor health in confirmation hearing &nb
items.content:
U.S. Navy used expired munitions as Iran war 'strains' resources
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Navy recoded and used munitions he described as expired during the Iran war.
Cao acknowledged that the war was "stressing our naval resources," as lawmakers questioned weapons stocks, ship deployments and sailor welfare.
Cao defended Navy's mental health support when questioned on eight suicide attempts abroad USS Lincoln.
WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 17: Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao testifies during a confirmation hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on November 17, 2026 in Washington, DC. Cao, nominated by President Trump, faced questions about the Iran War. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao's confirmation hearing before the Senate Armed Services Committee led to some heated exchanges as he was grilled about sailors' health and the Iran war.
The Navy changed condition codes on munitions previously classified as expired in order to use them, Cao told senators Tuesday, as lawmakers questioned the conflict's strain on weapons stocks and naval deployments. He also said the military had increased production of key weapons.
"When I was in uniform, we only produced 125 Tomahawks a year. Right now, we're well above 60 every month," he said, adding that the military was working to increase SM-6 missile production and bring in additional ammunition manufacturers.
Cao's confirmation hearing comes as the Republicans, who hold a majority in both the House and Senate, are coming to the end of their time in power in both houses. The Democratic Party flipped many seats in the midterm elections to win a comfortable majority in the next session starting in January. President Donald Trump's nominees for offices, and his legislative agenda, will face much tougher challenges then.
Cao said the Navy was accelerating work on unmanned surface vessels to relieve the 17 destroyers supporting the blockade of Iran's ships, in hopes of reducing the strain on the Fifth Fleet. But Senators still pointed to the war's effect on the Navy's resources.
"For the first time in many years, the United States has no forward-deployed carrier in the Pacific at this moment," Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.) noted.
Cao acknowledged that the war was "stressing our naval resources." However, he argued that the demonstration of combined American military capabilities had "really set China back on their heels," a characterization Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) disputed.
Lawmakers also pressed Cao on the war's financial costs, with Cao appearing to agree with Sen. Elizabeth Warren's (D-Mass.) estimate of approximately $32.5 million a day in costs to maintain the blockade on Iranian ports.
The demands of prolonged deployments have raised concerns about sailors' access to food and basic supplies, as Cao told senators that the destroyer USS Gonzalez had a week of rations remaining.
"Usually, I don't like them to go below two weeks of supplies," he said, while insisting the provisions were adequate and ships had never run out of food.
When Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) asked about reports of sailors losing 45 pounds, Cao stated that the food preferences might not be to certain sailors' liking.
He likened it to his children opening the refrigerator door and saying "there's nothing to eat here."
"Losing 45 pounds is more serious than just not liking the food. Our sailors are being asked to serve thousands of miles from home for months at a time. We have a responsibility to make sure they have what they need to do their jobs and stay healthy," Kelly posted on X .
Senators also questioned Cao about eight suicide attempts across the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group during its deployment. Cao defended the Navy's mental health support, describing the incidents as "eight suicide mitigations" because personnel had intervened.
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) called the term "mitigations" an "insult," saying they should be called suicide attempts.
The questioning followed an earlier acknowledgment by the top U.S. commander in the Middle East of mental health concerns aboard the Lincoln.
Cao pledged that the entire Department of the Navy would achieve a clean financial audit by the end of the fiscal year. The Pentagon has had nine consecutive failures to obtain a clean department-wide audit opinion, according to Reuters.
"We owe the American public to tell them exactly where their money is," he said.

items.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
items.summary: China worries the scandal could ramp up pressure on the US  to further restrict the sale of advanced chips.
items.content:
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.
Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.
Figure caption, Watch: Jensen Huang speaks to the BBC's Faisal Islam in 2025
Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.
The BBC has approached the White House for comment.
Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".
"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.
The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".
For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.
The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.
It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.
Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim , advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.
History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.
Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.
Image caption, The suspected Chinese spy balloon was shot down days after it was spotted over the US
But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.
The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.
"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.
"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.
The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.
"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.
Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.
China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.
Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.
The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.
He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.
Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.
The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.
It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.
Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.
One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.
Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.
That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share US official says Hormuz insurance hits $64m: Is the strait really open? on social media
The Liberia-flagged tanker Shenlong Suezmax, loaded with Saudi Arabian crude, arrives at a port in Mumbai, India, after transiting the Strait of Hormuz [File: Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters]
A senior United States Navy official has claimed that insurance costs for commercial ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz have soared to $64m for a single transit, highlighting the enormous economic toll of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao made the remarks during a Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing on Tuesday, as lawmakers questioned the cost of the war and its impact on freedom of navigation.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Is the US-Israel war on Iran turning into a ‘frozen conflict’?
list 2 of 3 Iranians fear more civilian infrastructure could be targeted in new US war
list 3 of 3 Trump warns Iran over reported ‘dirty bomb’ threat plans against Washington
After the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, Iran in effect closed the strait, allowing only some ships to pass while targeting those it says are unauthorised. This has raised the risks for shipping in the strait exponentially and caused severe shortages of oil, gas, fertiliser and other essential products from Gulf producers usually shipped via this route.
Cao’s claim has not been independently verified and challenges previously reported rises in insurance costs over the course of the nine-month-old conflict.
The remarks come as US President Donald Trump insists that the military campaign against Iran is effectively over, and that the US Navy is successfully escorting ships through the strait, even as new attacks on oil tankers and continued restrictions on shipping raise questions about whether one of the world’s most important energy waterways is really open.
The strait, the only sea route from the Gulf to the Arabian Sea and the open ocean beyond, carried about one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies before the war began.
Although some vessels are still navigating the waterway, shipping remains substantially below pre-war levels, while Iran and the US continue to impose competing restrictions.
(Al Jazeera) What did Hung Cao say in the Senate hearing?
During an exchange with Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, Cao said insurance costs for commercial vessels had risen dramatically since the conflict began.
He initially cited an insurance cost of $54,000 for a single crossing before clarifying that that was what insurance had previously cost, before the war. The cost now, he said, stood at $64m.
Slotkin responded by blaming the war for the increase, arguing that commercial vessels no longer enjoyed the same freedom of navigation they had before the conflict.
Cao also detailed the strain the war has placed on the US Navy, including prolonged deployments, deteriorating conditions and pressure on military resources.
Acting US Secretary of the US Navy Hung Cao [Saul Loeb/AFP] “This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our navy,” he told lawmakers.
Democrats accused Cao of being a Trump “yes man” on the US-Israeli war on Iran, and downplaying its toll on sailors’ mental health after eight suicide attempts on an aircraft carrier.
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from New York, asked him about a sailor who went overboard.
“Senator, that sailor was not trying to kill himself and he admitted that,” Cao told her, saying he used ‌a life preserver.
Gillibrand responded: “What was he trying to do? Swim to Guam?”
“I think you are minimising what mental health strain is on these service members,” Gillibrand replied, while dismissing Cao’s response as “inhumane”.
Cao’s $64m figure appears unusually high, even by the standards of wartime shipping insurance.
There is no independently verified evidence that $64m is the current insurance premium for a regular commercial vessel crossing the volatile strait.
“He gave no context. Is he talking about additional premiums for war risk insurance which are set as a percentage of hull value?” Michelle Bockmann, an analyst at maritime intelligence company Windward, told Al Jazeera.
“If so, it depends on the vessel type and the rate paid in order to get proper perspective.”
In July, a report published by S&P Global said that war-risk insurance premiums had climbed to between 7.5 and 10 percent of a ship’s hull value, compared with 1 to 3 percent previously.
It estimated that insurance for a tanker carrying 270,000 metric tonnes of crude could, therefore, cost approximately $21m.
Separately, Reuters news agency reported in September that the cost of moving an oil cargo through Hormuz had risen to roughly $10m-$20m, quoting an executive at Dubai’s Emirates National Oil Company (ENOC).
Regardless of whether it now costs $20m or $60m for insurance to transit the Strait of Hormuz, premiums have surged because ships face the possibility of being struck by missiles, drones or naval mines while passing through the waterway.
War-risk insurance covers vessels against losses arising from military conflict. Its price depends on the value of the vessel, the cargo and the likelihood of an attack.
Higher insurance costs can also feed into freight rates, fuel prices and the cost of goods transported around the world.
Technically, yes. But it remains far from fully and freely open as it was before the war.
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains approximately 65 percent below pre-war levels, according to the latest weekly report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
The UKMTO recorded 308 vessel crossings during the seven days ending November 11, comprising 139 outbound and 169 inbound journeys.
Nevertheless, Trump has repeatedly suggested that Washington has secured shipping through the strait by providing naval escorts and maintaining the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Meanwhile, Iran insists that it, in fact, controls the passage of shipping through the strait.
Tehran has demanded that vessels use approved routes and coordinate with its forces. It has also announced exemptions for ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar.
The route approved by Iran takes ships much closer to its own coastline than they used to sail, as the map below shows:
Alternative routes through the Strait of Hormuz – August 19 (Al Jazeera) The continuing dangers to ships ignoring Iran’s warnings were demonstrated this week.
On Monday, UKMTO reported two tanker attacks, including one near Oman that left a vessel disabled and its engine room on fire. The following day, Iranian forces claimed three additional tankers had struck naval mines.
On Tuesday, the US attacked targets on Iran’s Qeshm island , near Hormuz, following an Iranian drone attack targeting US military installations in Bahrain in recent days.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, said the strait could, therefore, hardly be considered open under normal circumstances.
“It is only open for business if mariners are prepared to take these risks, and it certainly isn’t open by any pre-war definition of the word,” he told Al Jazeera.
“It remains a miracle that we have avoided an energy crisis, and the longer this goes on, the more the alternatives will be developed.”
But Beauchamp said resolving the crisis would require Washington to confront the limits of its influence in the region.
“I can’t see a way that doesn’t involve conceding that the US does not have the ability to order things in the Middle East as it would wish,” he said.

Nvidia's quarterly revenue surges 103% amid board's decision on Jensen Huang
Humilis Investment Strategies CEO and CIO Brian Belski joins Taylor Riggs to analyze Nvidia's third-quarter earnings beat, showing a 103% year-over-year revenue surge. They also discuss the board's decision regarding Jensen Huang.
Nvidia has stopped shipping certain advanced artificial intelligence chips to China despite U.S. government approval for exports to eligible Chinese customers, and the company is excluding Chinese data center sales from its latest revenue forecast.
Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, without factoring in sales of AI computing chips and systems to China .
Colette Kress , Nvidia's interim CEO and longtime chief financial officer, said Tuesday that the company sold $2.4 billion worth of licensed Hopper-generation data center products to China during its fiscal third quarter, which ended Oct. 25.
"Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," Kress said in a statement.
JENSEN HUANG SAYS HE IS WILLING TO RETURN AS NVIDIA CEO, SAYING ‘I OWN MY MISTAKES COMPLETELY’
An Nvidia logo on the exterior of an office building is seen through an out-of-focus metal mesh fence in the foreground on November 16, 2026, in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China. (Cheng Xin/Getty Images)
Nvidia did not explain why the shipments stopped or say whether they would resume, leaving questions about the company's ability to serve the Chinese market despite changes to U.S. export rules.
The announcement came as Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of nearly $116 billion — more than double recorded a year earlier. Its data center business generated more than $107 billion in revenue, up 110% from the same period last year.
The shipment halt follows a decision by the U.S. government earlier this year to ease export restrictions on certain Nvidia processors destined for China.
In January, the Commerce Department revised its licensing policy for Nvidia's H200 chips, allowing export applications to be considered individually under specified security conditions. Those chips are part of Nvidia's Hopper family of processors, which are used to train and run advanced AI systems.
The policy shift followed discussions between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, along with efforts by Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, to expand the company's access to China.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks on stage during the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin, Germany, Oct. 19, 2026. (REUTERS/Lisi Niesner / Reuters Photos)
But U.S. export approval has not eliminated barriers to sales in China. Beijing has also restricted H200 imports as it seeks to reduce its dependence on American semiconductor technology.
The announcement also comes amid a leadership transition at Nvidia. Huang resigned last week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Kress was appointed interim CEO while continuing to serve as the company's chief financial officer.
Nvidia has not publicly clarified whether the shipment halt stems from U.S. licensing requirements, Chinese import restrictions or a separate business decision.

Oil Is Estimated to Ease in 2027 as Suppliers Adapt to Hormuz Disruption
Goldman Sachs Research forecasts that Brent crude will average $88 per barrel in 2027, easing to $78 by December, under its base case assumption that there are no major changes in the ongoing tensions in the Middle East.
The oil market likely tipped into a surplus in October 2026, and our analysts expect the surplus to reach 2 million barrels per day in 2027 amid a growing tanker fleet and new oil pipelines in the Middle East.
European LNG prices are also forecast to fall from €85/MWh today to an average of €45/MWh in 2027, although a colder-than-average winter could drive up prices.
Oil is forecast to ease gradually in 2027 as suppliers in the Middle East adapt to disruption from the war in Iran, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
Our commodities analysts expect benchmark Brent crude to average $88 per barrel in 2027 under their base case assumption of no definitive diplomatic breakthrough in Iran and no re-escalation with major long-term damage to oil infrastructure.
Under the same base case scenario, they project that Brent will fall from $93 per barrel today (as of November 17) to $78 by early December 2027 as a sizable surplus decreases Brent’s fair value from $90 per barrel today to the high $70s by the end of 2027. Goldman Sachs Research expects the risk premium in oil prices—which now appears relatively low—to gradually normalize.
Oil prices have risen less sharply this year than expected given the length of shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, writes Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research and head of oil research, in a report by his team.
In part, that was because of “remarkable oil market adaptation” to the war in Iran, Struyven adds. This included Gulf exporters redirecting supply through pipelines, dark exports, US Navy escorts, and ship-to-ship transfers.
The adaptation also included lower oil demand in response to higher prices—notably in China, which switched some of its energy demand to power and coal—and strong output of oil outside the Gulf, especially in Brazil.
“For 2027, we again expect a contest between high supply disruption risk and continued market adaptation,” Struyven writes.
The oil market likely tipped into a surplus in October 2026. The key driver was a rise in the supply of oil from the Persian Gulf in October—Goldman Sachs Research estimates that Persian Gulf crude exports recovered in October to their 2025 average, increasing 2 million barrels per day compared with the previous month.
Under Goldman Sachs Research’s base case scenario, our analysts expect the surplus to grow in 2027. They estimate that it will reach 2 million barrels per day in 2027 despite slowing growth in output from outside the Persian Gulf and continued supply disruptions.
Our analysts expect the recovery of output from the Gulf to trend higher as adaptation and added transportation resources, especially a larger tanker fleet and pipelines, support further growth in production.
Goldman Sachs Research expects an additional 3.8mb/d of pipeline capacity to come online over the next year as oil producers in the Middle East invest in pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz and transport oil directly to the Gulf of Oman, Red Sea, or Mediterranean Sea.
Struyven’s base case assumption sees 2027 oil output from the Gulf exceeding its 2025 average by 1.4 million barrels per day.
Global demand for oil took a hit from the conflict in the Middle East. Goldman Sachs Research expects global demand, with the exception of China, to recover to its pre-war trend once the availability and affordability of oil products improve, consistent with the rebounds in global demand following negative oil supply shocks in 2011 and 2022.
In China, our analysts expect persistent weakness in road fuel oil demand to drive 0.4 million barrels per day of “scarring” to global oil demand by the fourth quarter of 2027. The surge in use of electric passenger cars and trucks likely accelerated China’s energy transition, helping drive a 0.7 million barrel-per-day drop in Chinese gasoline and diesel demand in September 2026, year over year. Half of that decline is likely to persist, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
“Taken together, we estimate that China’s total oil demand peaked in 2025,” Struyven writes.
Goldman Sachs Research’s base case assumption is for European liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices to average €45 per megawatt hour in 2027 as supply from the Middle East continues to adapt. That would represent a decline from €85/MWh today (as of November 17).
“Yet even as supply adaptation has spread, it has worked less well for other commodities than for crude oil and has sharply raised shipping costs,” writes Samantha Dart, co-head of Global Commodities Research, who also leads the team’s global natural gas research.
The complexities of transporting LNG, which needs to be kept at very cold temperatures, make ship-to-ship transfers harder than for oil. And because it is more flammable than oil, transporting LNG can be more dangerous for the crew in the event of an attack, Dart explains.
European LNG could rise to near €150/MWh in the first quarter of 2027 if Persian Gulf LNG exports average 25%-30% of pre-war levels this winter and if Europe's winter turns out one standard deviation colder (0.7° Celsius) than average, Dart writes. If Gulf LNG exports stall at around 35% of pre-war levels through end-2027, her team estimates that European LNG prices would average €104/MWh in 2027.

China Gas Upsizes Long-Term LNG Supply with U.S. Venture Global
China Gas Holdings Limited, a major Chinese natural gas distributor and operator, has doubled the LNG volumes it will receive from U.S. exporter Venture Global under a recent 20-year deal.
China Gas and Venture Global on Wednesday announced the execution of an increased Sales and Purchase Agreement (SPA) for the total purchase of 1.0 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) of U.S. LNG from Venture Global for 20 years starting in 2030.
This agreement upsizes the previous SPA announced in September 2026 for the purchase of 0.5 MTPA by another newly agreed 0.5 MTPA, Venture Global said.
China Gas has contracted in recent years other LNG supply with U.S. exporters , including Venture Global.
The latest announcement of doubled volumes to 1 MTPA takes Venture Global's total current long-term offtake with China Gas to as much as 3.0 MTPA under 20-year agreements supplied across Venture Global's portfolio.
"Venture Global is pleased to continue growing our LNG partnership with China Gas, a leading natural gas operator in China, and help meet the country's growing energy needs with reliable, low-cost American LNG from across our Louisiana projects," said Venture Global CEO Mike Sabel.
Liu Ming Hui, Chairman and President of China Gas, commented, "This agreement supports China Gas's strategy to build a global LNG trading business that connects reliable supply sources with markets where gas demand is growing."
Despite a near-term decline in China's LNG imports due to the high spot prices following the Iran war, the long-term demand prospects remain intact.
Venture Global, for its part, is boosting its supply as it just launched commercial operations of the first phase of its second LNG export project, Plaquemines LNG.
With soaring LNG prices this year and U.S. LNG in high demand amid the lack of Qatari cargoes, Venture Global booked record sales and earnings for the third quarter of 2026.

items.title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring sales
items.summary: The AI chip giant reported strong quarterly earnings on Tuesday after the dramatic exit of Jensen Huang.
items.content:
Image caption, Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress
By Kali Hays ,Â  Technology reporter Â  and Â  Osmond Chia ,Â  Business reporter
Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this."
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him."
Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (Â£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.
The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.
How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.
"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Figure caption, Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.
The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.
Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.
"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."
Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.
The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.
Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

Two-thirds of Americans now say they disapprove of President Donald Trump’s handling of the war between Russia and Ukraine, while three-in-ten say they approve, according to a Pew Research Center survey of 10,247 adults conducted Nov. 9-15.

These findings come as Trump prepares to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in China on Thursday.
Around four-in-ten Americans say Trump is favoring Russia too much in the conflict, while a much smaller share (7%) say he is favoring Ukraine too much. Another 21% say Trump is striking the right balance, and 33% say they are not sure.
There continues to be a wide partisan gap over whether the United States has a responsibility to help Ukraine defend itself. Among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, 65% say the U.S. does have this responsibility, while 34% of Republicans and Republican leaners say the same.
33% of Americans say Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is a major threat to U.S. interests – little changed over the past two years. Democrats are about twice as likely as Republicans to call this a major threat (44% vs. 21%).
59% of Republicans approve of Trump’s approach to the war, while 91% of Democrats disapprove.

items.title: Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe
items.summary: The $60m (£45m) plane was destroyed in an hours-long raid by an anti-war protester, according to the FBI.
items.content:
Image caption, The military plane, seen above, was effectively destroyed by the vandalism
US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (Â£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly sneaked onto the tarmac of an airport in Ireland.
Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is accused of doing extensive research before he allegedly used chemicals and various tools - including an axe - to damage a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules parked at Shannon Airport near Limerick.
American prosecutors have charged him with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
O'Corrain is not currently in US custody, according to the Associated Press news agency, and it is unclear whether he has a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.
In filings unsealed by prosecutors in New York on Tuesday, agents from the FBI argued that the act jeopardised US national security. They say the plane was parked at the airport while en route to another country on a US military assignment.
"As alleged, Daithi O'Corrain carried out a deliberate, planned attack against a US military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations," prosecutors said in a court filing.
"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr, explaining O'Corrain "spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict."
Officials say that the suspect planned extensively for the 11 April 2026 raid, and brought tools with him for the demolition, which took place over several hours.
He entered the plane by breaking a locking mechanism, officials say, then used straps to close the doors before covering the windows.
"O'Corrain then proceeded to inflict severe damage to the interior of the Aircraft by, among other things, cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines within the Aircraft, crimping a liquid oxygen line within the Aircraft, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft's cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft's air ducts," the US indictment says.
He also used gallium, a substance that can erode aluminum and steel, ball bearings which he poured in the fuel tank, and an axe which he used to puncture the exterior of the plane.
He was caught by airport crew, and filmed standing on top of the plane. He was arrested at the scene, and charged by Ireland's national police with causing criminal damages.
Image caption, O'Corrain seen standing on the rear of the aircraft in a handout from the US Department of Justice
The US charges say that he had planned well, because he avoided cutting a line that would have risked causing massive explosion.
According to the Limerick Post , external , O'Corrain is from Cork City. Supporters have described him as an anti-war activist.
Shannon Airport is a key hub for US military personnel, and is frequently the scene of anti-war protests. It was used by President Donald Trump in September for his visit to Ireland.
US prosecutors note that there have been several breaches there in recent years by protesters, including in May 2025 when three people drove a van through a perimeter fence , and then again later that month when a US airplane was sprayed with paint, making it temporarily inoperable.

items.title: Who speaks for Europe abroad? Not its top diplomat
items.summary: EU leaders’ decision to exclude the bloc’s foreign policy chief from their negotiating lineup for Russia peace talks reveals how national turf wars undermine Brussels’ global ambitions• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereThe EU, we are repeatedly told, wants (and needs) to be a global player, a geopolitical
items.content:
‘We decide for ourselves who will represent us’, Ursula Von Der Leyen in Dublin last week. Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA
‘We decide for ourselves who will represent us’, Ursula Von Der Leyen in Dublin last week. Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA
EU leaders’ decision to exclude the bloc’s foreign policy chief from their negotiating lineup for Russia peace talks reveals how national turf wars undermine Brussels’ global ambitions
Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
T he EU, we are repeatedly told, wants (and needs) to be a global player, a geopolitical heavyweight capable of shaping its own foreign and security policies – or at the very least, speaking with one clear, unambiguous voice on the world stage.
Last Friday’s summit in Dublin , when leaders debated who should represent the bloc in talks aimed at ending Russia’s war on Ukraine – the gravest security crisis the EU has faced in decades – showed once again that it is unlikely to find such a voice anytime soon.
The EU has a chief diplomat: she is called Kaja Kallas, she is a former Estonian prime minister, and she was appointed the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, and a European Commission vice-president, in 2024.
In theory, Kallas should embody this more assertive Europe. But as the US-mediated talks accelerate, EU leaders have – despite Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s pleas for the bloc to field a single negotiator – locked her out of the room.
Instead, alongside US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Europe is being represented by a seven-strong team: European Council president António Costa, Commission president Ursula von der Leyen , and representatives from the E5 powers: France, Germany, Britain, Poland, and Italy, working with Nato.
On paper, Kallas’s job description is straightforward and twofold. She chairs the Foreign Affairs Council, the monthly decision-making forum where national foreign ministers meet to agree on common EU foreign policy, sanctions and crisis responses.
She also runs the European External Action Service (EEAS), the bloc’s permanent diplomatic corps and de facto foreign ministry, made up of civil servants and over 140 embassies around the world that carry out day-to-day EU diplomacy on the ground.
In practice, being the face of EU foreign policy – a role created by the Lisbon Treaty in 2009 to answer Henry Kissinger’s famous if apocryphal question “Who do I call when I want to talk to Europe?” – is, as one commentator puts it, a “poisoned chalice”.
Jennifer Rankin in Brussels tells me: “Personally, I think Kallas has an impossible job: having to represent the positions of 27 member states that often disagree on foreign policy, and don’t want to cede real decision making on it to the EU.”
Relations between Kallas and von der Leyen – who critics accuse of sharing exactly the same kind of power-hoarding and centralising instincts as some EU national leaders – have been particularly difficult.
That friction has been aggravated by active proposals in Brussels to overhaul the bloc’s whole diplomatic service, folding parts of the EEAS and key foreign policy powers directly into the Commission president’s remit.
On Friday, when the Dublin summit convened, Kallas was unequivocal : leaders had agreed in 2024, when it was clear there would have to be talks with Russia, “that I’mthe one who is representing Europe in foreign and security policy,” she said.
But when Costa announced the bloc’s negotiators in Dublin, Kallas wasn’t among them. So why did the 27 capitals bypass the person they hired for the job?
Three explanations are doing the diplomatic rounds . First, several western European capitals view the Estonian envoy as too overtly, and fiercely, anti-Russian.
Second, there is a much deeper reflex at play: the EU’s big member states simply refuse to cede real foreign policy power to Brussels. Paris and Berlin in particular resist a single EU envoy, clearly preferring to protect their own seats at the table.
Third, diplomats point to a wider trend for the kind of international questions once handled by foreign ministers being taken over by premiers or presidents.
Whatever the reason, von der Leyen’s defence of the decision was brisk: “We decide for ourselves who will represent us, and we made that decision today,” she said . Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has also argued that intergovernmental formats like the E3 – France, Germany and the UK – are “a well-established format” and “I see absolutely no problem with keeping it that way.”
Others, though, were less happy. Spain and Lithuania both criticised the team approach. “Europe needs one voice,” said Lithuania’s foreign minister , Kęstutis Budrys. “We cannot speak with 27 microphones. We need one.”
Kaja Kallas is supposed to be the face of EU foreign policy. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters All this may seem rather inside-the-Brussels-beltway stuff. But beneath it lies a real, and important debate over whether the EU will ever be a global actor, or be fated to remain a disjointed collection of national voices.
Defenders of the Dublin decision argue that hard security and ending the war are issues that belong to the EU’s major military and financial powers, not supranational officials: bringing the big beasts to the table provides the real geopolitical heft.
One EU diplomat said the problem was that EU institutions “do not have sufficient political legitimacy in the eyes of voters. And this matters big time. The E5 solution is an attempt to bridge that gap.”
But critics see a damaging own goal, and a profound hypocrisy. Brussels commenter Dave Keating argues there is a fatal contradiction inherent in Europe’s integration.
Member states “know what the right thing to do is in the abstract, so they create these positions and institutions to make a stronger EU,” he says. “But then … they undermine [them] … because they always give in to the urge not to hand over power to someone else.”
By choosing to field what Keating called a “European cacophony” that would inevitably be dismissed as irrelevant by Moscow and Washington, leaders proved Kallas’s job “is not real, and the EU doesn’t actually have a foreign policy”, he said.
Jennifer is slightly less damning. “I think the E5+ format could be seen as a realistic answer to represent the EU as it is, not the idealised union of the treaties,” she said. “It needn’t be a cacophony if everyone in the room has the same message.”
So far, on Ukraine at least, there is a large degree of consensus. But if, for example, Marine Le Pen becomes French president, all bets are off,” says Jennifer.
For her part, Kallas has put a brave face on it , insisting she will focus on “substance” while leaders handle “format”. But the suspicion remains: Europe’s leaders want the bloc to be a global power, but won’t let anyone else speak for them.
Until they do, the risk is that the EU will be stuck on the diplomatic sidelines, forever punching below its geopolitical weight.

items.content:
Duyuk al-Tahta, east of Jericho, West Bank, where Fadha Wadha was killed. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were also wounded. Photograph: Issam Rimawi/Anadolu/Getty Images
Duyuk al-Tahta, east of Jericho, West Bank, where Fadha Wadha was killed. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were also wounded. Photograph: Issam Rimawi/Anadolu/Getty Images
Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say
Bullet hit 72-year-old Fadha Wadha in head outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, in the West Bank, say residents
A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in a village near Jericho where settlers have recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta in the occupied West Bank when she was struck in the head by a bullet as Israeli settlers fired towards Palestinian houses, according to testimonies from residents. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were wounded by gunfire.
Abu Younis, a cousin of Wadha’s husband, told the Guardian that the violence had begun when a group of settlers attacked a young boy they accused of entering a courtyard seized from its Palestinian residents.
Dozens of Israeli settlers, some of them armed, moved into eight buildings in al-Duyuk al-Tahta two weeks ago with the backing of the settler organisation Nachala and a regional council representing illegal settlements in the central West Bank.
Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
“A vehicle carrying settlers chased him,” Younis said. “There were about 15 settlers in several vehicles. They began firing indiscriminately, killing the woman.”
Witnesses said Palestinian residents began to throw stones to defend themselves, as more settlers arrived at the scene, shooting at civilians and injuring six men.
Wadha’s son, Arafat Fidhat, was wounded after he rushed to the scene after learning that his mother had been shot. His wife, Naama Fidhat, told Reuters he was in shock when he accidentally collided with a parked car belonging to one of the settlers.
Witnesses said the vehicle was empty at the time, but that settlers responded by opening fire, wounding Arafat in the torso.
Mourners attend the funeral of Wadha Fadha, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman killed by Israeli settlers, near Jericho. Photograph: Jamal Awad/Reuters Naama Fidhat said her husband was being taken to a hospital in Ramallah when Israeli soldiers stopped the ambulance and arrested him. She said Israeli soldiers also arrested their son, Wadha’s grandson, early the following morning.
“What did we do? We didn’t do anything,” she said. “This is our house, they were the ones who came with weapons … we were unarmed, we were sleeping.”
The Israeli military said a group of Palestinians in ​a car “accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it”. It said the Palestinians exited the vehicle and attacked the Israelis, who opened fire at the Palestinians. “There are Israeli and Palestinian ​casualties in the incident,” the military said.
The arrival of the Israeli settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta had raised fears among Palestinian residents who have faced repeated attacks in the area.
The Binyamin regional council, which covers 47 illegal settlements, claimed the properties in the village had been bought from Palestinians, but Jericho’s governor, Hussein Hamayel, disputed the claim, saying the land belonged to the state and could not legally be sold.
Human rights activists said settlers had assaulted and robbed two Israeli activists and shot a Palestinian man in the leg during the takeover earlier this month.
Ed Miliband announces first sanctions on Israeli firms working in West Bank
“Since the settlers moved into the area on 4 November our lives have been turned upside down,” Younis told the Guardian. “We used to live peacefully and safely on our farms, but since the settlers arrived, our lives have become a living hell. I own 53 dunams [5.3 hectares] of farmland with greenhouses, but we are no longer allowed to access them. We have suffered devastating financial losses, and now people are being killed as well.”
There has been a sharp ​rise in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the West Bank, territory Israel captured in the 1967 six-day war. UN bodies and most ​countries deem the settlements illegal, which Israel disputes.
On Tuesday, Suleiman Abu Srour, a photographer for the Palestinian news agency Wafa, was beaten by Israeli soldiers while covering events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta . Wafa said he suffered fractures and bruises, was detained for six hours and had his phone confiscated before being released.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

items.title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
items.summary: The AI company behind Claude is about to sell its shares on the US stock market - making its founders very rich.
items.content:
Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Image caption, Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic
By Tom Espiner Â  and Â  Lucy Hooker ,Â  Business reporters
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.
If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.
Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Image source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Image source, Cornell Watson/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Image source, Peerapon Boonyakiat/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.
Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.
Image source, Chris J. Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.
His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.
Image source, Alberto PIZZOLI / AFP via Getty Images
Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.
But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.
Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.
He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.
The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.
Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.
McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.
He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

Stock Market Today: Strong Nvidia Results Fail to Boost Major Indexes as Investors Await Anthropic IPO; Dow Drops 600 Points
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite came into today's session on four-day losing streaks.
Credit: Spencer Platt / Getty Images Major stock indexes are losing ground Wednesday despite a strong earnings report from AI chipmaker Nvidia, as investors prepare for Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was recently down 1.2%, or more than 600 points, after the blue-chip index dropped 850 point yesterday . The benchmark S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite, which entered today's session on four-day losing streaks, were down 0.6% and 0.2%, respectively. U.S. stocks have been under pressure in recent weeks amid mounting concerns about the sustainability of the AI-related gains that have unpinned the market's record performance in recent years.
Some of those concerns appeared to ease following a blockbuster earnings report last night from Nvidia (NVDA), the chipmaker at the forefront of the AI boom. Nvidia shares jumped in early trading today but were down 2% recently, despite quarterly results and guidance from the company that blew past analysts' expectations. The stock has been hammered recently as investors weigh how the swift downfall of former CEO Jensen Huang could affect the company and the broader AI buildout.
Trading in other chip stocks is volatile this morning. Shares of Nvidia rivals Broadcom (AVGO) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) were up 3% and 1%, respectively, while Marvell Technology (MRVL), Intel (INTC) and Micron (MU) dropped more than 2%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was down nearly 1% recently, after bouncing between gains and losses in the first several hours of trading.
The AI trade could get a boost this week with the IPO of the company behind the Claude chatbot. Anthropic is expected to announce the pricing of its shares today, with trading set to start tomorrow on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT". Anthropic is expected to have a market value well above $1 trillion when it starts trading, making it one of the largest companies in the world by market capitalization.
Shares of UnitedHealth (UNH) were leading decliners on the Dow this morning, falling 6% amid rising concerns about regulatory scrutiny of health insurers. Shares of Humana (HUM) were also down 6%.
Mining stocks Freeport-McMoRan (FCX) and Newmont (NEM) paced S&P 500 decliners, dropping, more than 7% each as the precious metals prices declined.
Meanwhile, shares of several retailers were on the move as a busy week of earnings reports from the sector continues. Shares of TJX Companies (TJX) jumped 10% to lead S&P 500 advancers, while Target (TGT) was up 6% after the retailers reported results that topped Wall Street expectations. Lowe's (LOW) shares were down 1% as a disappointing outlook overshadowed strong quarterly numbers. The big report of the week comes tomorrow, when Walmart ( WMT ) is scheduled to release its results.
In other markets, gold futures were down 2.8% at $3,755 an ounce this morning, trading at their lowest level in nearly 14 months, while WTI oil futures slipped 2.1% to $84.15 per barrel. Bitcoin continued its recent slide, trading at $63,000.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which affects interest rates on all sorts of consumer loans, was at 5.07%, down from yesterday's close of 5.12%. The yield has risen in recent weeks amid expectations the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again next month.
