A top Federal Reserve official warned Wednesday that the central bank may need to take more drastic action to tame inflation.
"I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out, it's not just concentrated in a few categories," Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in an interview with CNBC . "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions."
Waller suggested that the Fed might need to "shock people," indicating that the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee may need to raise the benchmark interest rate by half a percentage point at its next meeting in December.
Christopher Waller speaking at an event hosted by Bloomberg News in New Dehli last month.
Credit: Prakash Singh / Bloomberg / Getty Images The Fed last month opted to stand pat on rates, after raising the key rate by a quarter point in September, which was the first time it had done so in three years.
Inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% target, and recent data hasn't indicated that price pressures are easing. Market participants are pricing in a 100% chance that the FOMC will raise rates next month, but very few expect that that it would be more than quarter-point adjustment. It's been four years since the Fed raised the benchmark rate more than a quarter point in a single meeting.
The minutes from last month's FOMC meeting are due to be released this afternoon, and other voting members of the policy committee are due to speak later today.
Anthropic to Join Ranks of Most Valuable Public Companies
Anthropic is finalizing the share price for its IPO , and the numbers may top its initial price range, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The AI lab is slated to make its trading debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, with shares trading under the ticker "ANT."
Anthropic previously estimated shares would sell for $70 to $78, which would give the company behind Claude a $1.4 trillion valuation. But strong investor demand could lead Anthropic to lift share prices above $80, which would put its valuation closer to $1.5 or $1.6 trillion, The Journal said.
At that level, Anthropic would immediately join the list of the top 10 largest companies by market capitalization . SpaceX (SPCX), which carried out its IPO in June, has a market value of just under $2 trillion.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were down 0.1%.

items.content:
Dow Drops Nearly 860 Points as Stock Market Selloff Deepens Ahead of Nvidia Earnings
U.S. stocks fell Tuesday as investors pulled back ahead of Nvidia's earnings report, while renewed warnings about higher interest rates added pressure to a market already struggling with doubts about the artificial intelligence boom.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 859.71 points, or 1.67%, to 50,748.46, according to preliminary closing figures. The S&P 500 lost 75.96 points, or 1.02%, to 7,341.23, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 180.42 points, or 0.74%, to 24,329.34. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq recorded their fourth consecutive declines, their longest losing streaks since September.
The losses followed a bruising Monday session, when the Dow shed about 739 points, the S&P 500 fell 1.9%, and the Nasdaq tumbled 2.5%. Across the two sessions, the Dow has surrendered nearly 1,600 points. Monday's retreat also hit smaller companies, with the Russell 2000 falling 1.7%.
Tuesday's selling extended beyond the technology companies that have dominated market attention. All 11 S&P 500 sectors were lower during afternoon trading. Software shares weighed on the Dow, while Salesforce and UnitedHealth were among the stocks contributing to its decline. The index briefly fell about 1,000 points before recovering some ground.
Nvidia remained the central corporate event on investors' calendars. Its quarterly results, scheduled after the closing bell, carried implications for chipmakers, cloud computing companies and the broader network of businesses tied to AI spending.
The report arrives as investors reassess the industry's momentum. Tuesday's session reflected mounting caution ahead of Nvidia's first earnings release without Jensen Huang leading the company. Anthropic's anticipated stock market debut added another major test of demand for AI investments later this week.
St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem said on Tuesday that the economy would likely require multiple rate increases before spring 2027 to bring inflation under control. He argued that the current benchmark rate, between 3.75% and 4%, could be as much as one percentage point below the level needed to restore price stability.
Higher borrowing costs can squeeze corporate earnings, discourage expansion and make bonds more competitive with stocks. They also affect the value investors assign to future profits, a particularly important consideration for growth companies whose valuations depend on earnings expected years from now.
October retail sales increased 0.2% from the previous month, while sales excluding autos and gasoline rose 0.5%. The figures suggested consumers continued spending, even as investors weighed whether persistent demand could complicate the inflation outlook.

Trump-Putin: Ukraine allies reject U.S. criticism of deep strikes
Germany and the U.K. pushed back against U.S. criticism of Ukraine’s deep strikes inside Russia, exposing a rift over Kyiv’s war strategy.
U.S. defense official Elbridge Colby said the strikes had not helped end the war or slow Russia’s advance. German and British officials said they had weakened Russia’s war effort.
The dispute comes ahead of a planned meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi, as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian oil, logistics and military targets, including the Kerch Bridge.
German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius (R) speaks with U.S. Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby (L) before the start of a meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group at NATO Headquarters on November 17, 2026 in Brussels, Belgium.
Germany and the U.K. have pushed back against U.S. criticism of Ukraine's deep strike campaign inside Russia, underscoring tensions between Washington and European allies over Kyiv's war strategy.
The clash comes ahead of a highly anticipated trilateral meeting on Thursday between U.S. President Donald Trump , Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China.
Geopolitical flashpoints such as trade, artificial intelligence and nuclear weapons are expected to be a major focus of Trump, Putin and Xi's meeting, with external observers closely monitoring any discussion of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Speaking at NATO's headquarters in Belgium on Tuesday, U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby likened Ukraine's deep strikes inside Russia to a spectacle, adding that they "have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia's advances on the front line."
The Pentagon policy chief acknowledged Ukraine's mid-range strike campaign using novel drone technologies and tactics to deny Russian advances on the front line has proven "very effective."
He added that Ukraine's Armed Forces gained more territory than Russia for the second consecutive month in October.
However, Colby said Ukraine's deep strikes targeting "civilian infrastructure," citing Russia's biggest online retailer Wildberries , "have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate."
Kyiv has said that warehouses targeted by Ukrainian drones were involved in providing Russian forces with drone components, navigation equipment and other military components. Wildberries and the Kremlin have denied the company is involved in Russia's war in Ukraine.
Xi-Trump-Putin summit will be a 'photo-op' that elevates China: David Roche
Asked whether he shared Colby's position on Ukraine's deep strike campaign inside Russia, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said criticizing strikes designed to destroy strategic military and military-use targets in Russia "is quite a stupid thing, I think."
"Instead of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on civil energy, water and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said at a news conference.
British Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting echoed those comments, saying it is "not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war."
He added: "There is no doubt in my mind that it has helped to degrade Putin's war machine, buying time and saving lives."
Trump has previously called on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks were responsible for a global shortage.
Ukraine has stepped up its strikes on Russian oil facilities and logistics infrastructure in recent months, seeking to raise the cost of the war for Moscow after more than 4½ years of conflict.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday lauded an "unprecedented operation" targeting the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea in what marked a symbolic blow to the Kremlin's war effort.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte speaks to the press upon arrival for a meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group at NATO headquarters, in Brussels, on November 17, 2026.
A coordinated drone and missile strike on the bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian forces and is one of Putin's signature projects, damaged the crossing.
In response, Russia said the bridge would be restored and "will be even better than before."

items.summary: New York Fed’s Williams rules out jumbo rate hike for December  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
New York Fed's Williams rules out jumbo rate hike for December
New York Federal Reserve president John Williams poured cold water on the central bank making a jumbo 50-basis-point interest rate hike next month but noted that the Fed does have to get inflation down.
"I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action," Williams said during a Q&A with Axios in New York.
Williams acknowledged that the data is sending a "pretty clear signal."
"We still have our work to do to make sure that we bring inflation back down to 2% in a timely way and in a sustained manner," he said.
Williams' comments come as the latest inflation data shows price growth that is surprisingly higher than expected. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October , compared with expectations of 0.3%, marking a slight cooldown from September's 0.6% gain. "Core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, compared with expectations of 0.2% and unchanged from September.
A reading of the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heated up in September, with the core Personal Consumption Expenditures index rising 3.1% , up a tenth of a percentage point from 3% in August.
Markets have been weighing a larger rate hike ever since inflation readings came in hot. Fed governor Chris Waller said ahead of the CPI report that if consumer prices were higher than expected, he'd consider a move of 50 basis points.
After Williams spoke on Tuesday, investors still saw a 98% chance the Fed hikes by 25 basis points in December.
Williams wouldn't characterize inflation as broadening, but acknowledged a continuation of higher price increases on imported goods where tariffs are in place and energy prices that are being passed on. He also pointed to AI investments causing certain prices, such as semiconductors, to rise. Williams identified AI as the most likely "persistent" factor of inflation.
How many rate hikes and at what pace the Fed must implement them will depend on what's happening in AI, Williams said. He noted that a lot of strength in the economy is coming from AI, and consumer spending is being boosted by a strong stock market.
"If those continue, I think that that's a factor that will argue that we may need to raise rates more at the same time those factors have been pushing inflation up. But there's just a great deal of uncertainty," he said.

In separate remarks, Waller endorsed innovation in tokenized payments but warned that blockchain-based finance needs reliable settlement infrastructure and clearer accountability.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller wants the central bank to get more aggressive with interest rate hikes, arguing that stubborn inflation may require a 50-basis-point increase in December rather than the smaller move investors expect.
Speaking during a CNBC interview Wednesday, Waller said the Fed must either deliver a half-percentage-point increase at its December 8-9 meeting or explicitly signal that another hike will follow in January.
“You might need to, like, shock people,” Waller said, referring to the central bank's efforts to prevent businesses and consumers from accepting inflation near 3% as normal.

Markets remain less convinced that the Fed will move that aggressively in December. Futures pricing Wednesday morning showed roughly a 95% probability of a 25-basis-point increase and only about a 5% probability of a half-point move
The prospect of higher borrowing costs has been particularly painful for crypto investors. Higher interest rates make Treasury securities and other interest-bearing investments more competitive with speculative assets, while tighter financial conditions can reduce the money available for riskier bets.
Bitcoin has already suffered a sharp selloff amid the changing rate outlook. As Decrypt previously covered , persistent inflation fears have coincided with withdrawals from spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds and weakening technical indicators, adding pressure to an already fragile market.
Waller also wants blockchain finance to work with banks
Waller's increasingly hawkish monetary-policy stance comes alongside a more accommodating view of blockchain networks, although he sees established financial infrastructure as essential to its adoption.
In a separate November 17 speech at The Clearing House Annual Conference in New York, Waller discussed how tokenization—the representation of financial assets on digital networks—could reshape payments and securities markets. That speech focused on financial technology rather than interest-rate policy.
He pointed to a growing convergence between traditional markets and blockchain platforms, with banks and payment providers experimenting with tokenized deposits, stablecoins, and programmable transactions.
Waller described how tokenized money could allow investors to purchase securities outside conventional trading hours, with payments and assets changing hands simultaneously through smart contracts.
But he rejected the idea that the development of blockchain-based markets necessarily makes existing payment infrastructure obsolete.
“Central bank money need not be used in every transaction or on every platform, but its presence at the foundation of the system is essential,” Waller said.
